newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM travels to Okinawa in symbolic gesture.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM travels to Okinawa in symbolic gesture.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto flew to Okinawa on Wednesday in a political gesture to soften opposition to a revision of a land expropriation law for U.S. military bases.

Along with leaders of five other political parties, Hashimoto attended the funeral of Chobyo Yara, the first governor of Okinawa after the southern island reverted to Japan in 1972 following 27 years of U.S. military occupation.
Hashimoto's gesture was greeted with scepticism by some Okinawans, who resent the presence of U.S. bases and what they see as neglect by Tokyo.

"Today he prays for peace in Okinawa, tomorrow he'll inflict pain on Okinawa (with the land legislation)," said a retired teachers union official. "Mr Yara is not happy to be used for political purposes."
Hashimoto, whose cabinet will formally approve the expropriation bill on Thursday, did not hold talks with local leaders during his short stay in Okinawa.
But after returning to the capital he met with Ichiro Ozawa, head of the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) to seek its support for the legislation.

At stake is the proposed revision of land expropriation laws that Hashimoto says he needs to meet a May 14 deadline on expiration of leases on private land currently taken up by U.S. military bases on Okinawa.
Private land for U.S. bases is expropriated by the Japanese government, not the U.S. military itself.
Without revisions the government would be "illegally" occupying the land -- a state of affairs Hashimoto has said the government must avoid at all costs.
The legislation will, in effect, give the Japanese government a temporary extension of its leases on land occupied by U.S. bases after current contracts expire.
Hashimoto said he would submit the bill to parliament on Thursday. The ruling Liberal Democratic Party's two parliamentary allies agreed to start deliberations on April 7.

According to media reports, although Hashimoto's LDP lacks a majority in either chamber of parliament, the bill is likely to clear the legislature with the help of small parties and independent lawmakers.
The deadline is on leases on land owned by 3,000 people who are refusing to renew the contracts. Another 29,000 landowners have agreed to renew.
They are a series of mainly small plots of land totalling 36 hectares (89 acres) on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base.
The case is now before an Okinawan land expropriation committee, whose decision to renew leases was not expected before the May deadline.
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015 but Tokyo strongly opposes such a move.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota has bitterly opposed the proposed revisions.
The row between the central and Okinawan governments over U.S. bases flared up in September 1995 when three U.S. servicemen were arrested for the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl.
